Hezekiah gave all the silver found in the house of the Lord and in the treasuries of the king’s palace.
At that time Hezekiah broke apart the doors of the Lord’s temple and the doorposts that Hezekiah king of Judah had covered with gold, and gave them to the king of Assyria.

The king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah with a large army against Jerusalem. They went up and came to Jerusalem and stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool, which is on the road to the fuller’s field.
They called out to Hezekiah, and Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator, Shebna, the chief scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, who was in charge of the records, came out to them.
The Rabshakeh said to them, “Tell Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: What is this confidence on which you rely?”
“But if you say, ‘Words of the lips, counsel, and strength are needed for war,’ then on whom have you relied, that you have rebelled against me?
Look, you are relying on Egypt, that broken reed of a staff. If a man leans on it, it will pierce his hand and wound him. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who rely on him.”
And if you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord God,’ is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem’?
Now, please, make a wager with my lord, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses if you can provide riders for them.
How can you withstand even one governor among the least of my master’s servants, when you rely on Egypt for chariots and horses?
And have we now come up against this place to destroy it without the Lord? The Lord said to me, ‘Go up against that land and destroy it.’

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah son of Asaph said to the Rabshakeh, ‘Speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak in Hebrew within hearing of the people on the wall.’

The Rabshakeh said to them, ‘Did my master send me to your master and to you to speak these words? Was it not to the men sitting on the wall, who will eat their own dung and drink their own urine along with you?’
Then the Rabshakeh stood and shouted loudly in Hebrew, saying, ‘Hear the message of the great king, the king of Assyria!
This is what the king says: Do not let Hezekiah make you overconfident, for he cannot rescue you from my hands.
And do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the Lord by saying, “The Lord will surely deliver us, and this city will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.”

Do not listen to Hezekiah, for this is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then each of you may eat from his own vine and his own fig tree and drink water from his own well,

until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of wheat and wine, of vineyards and bread, a land of olive trees, oil, and honey, so that you may live and not die. Do not listen to Hezekiah, for he deceives you when he says, “The Lord will deliver us.”
Have the gods of the nations ever delivered their own lands from the hands of the king of Assyria?
Where is the god of Hamath and Arpad? And where is the god of Sepharvaim, of the cities of Hena and Ivvah? Did they deliver Samaria from my hands?
Which of all the gods of the lands has delivered its land from my hands, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem from my hands?’
But they remained silent and gave him no answer, for the king had commanded, ‘Do not answer him.’

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the chief administrator, Shebna the chief scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, who was in charge of the records, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported the Rabshakeh’s words to him.
When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and went into the house of the Lord.
He sent Eliakim the chief administrator, Shebna the chief scribe, and the elders among the priests, dressed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
They said to him, ‘This is what Hezekiah says: This day is a day of distress, rebuke, and provocation, for the children have reached the point of birth, but there is no strength to give birth.

Perhaps your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master, the king of Assyria, sent to insult the living God, and rebuke him for the words that the Lord your God has heard. Offer a prayer for the remnant that is left.’
So King Hezekiah’s servants came to Isaiah.
Isaiah said to them, ‘Tell your master this: Thus says the Lord: Do not be afraid because of the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me.’
Look, I will put a spirit in him, and he will hear a report and return to his own land. I will bring him down by the sword in his own land.
The Rabshakeh returned and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had departed from Lachish.
He heard it said about Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, “Look, he has come out to fight against you.” He returned and sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying:
“Speak this way to Hezekiah, king of Judah: Do not let your God, in whom you trust, make you proud by saying that Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.
Look, you yourself have heard everything the kings of Assyria did to all the lands, condemning them to destruction. And will you be delivered?
Did the gods of the nations whom my fathers destroyed deliver them—Gozan, Haran, Raphath, and the people of Eden by the seashore?
Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?”
Hezekiah took the letters from the messengers and read them. Then he went up to the house of the Lord, and Hezekiah spread them out before the Lord.
Hezekiah prayed before the Lord and said, “Lord, God of Israel, enthroned upon the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth.”
“Incline your ear, Lord, and hear. Open your eyes, Lord, and see. Hear the words of Sennacherib, which he sent to insult the living God.
For truly, Lord, the kings of Assyria have devastated the nations and their lands,
and they gave their gods to the fire, because they were not gods but the work of human hands, wood and stone. So they destroyed them.
And now, Lord our God, deliver us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the Lord God.”
Isaiah son of Amoz sent word to Hezekiah, saying, “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have heard the prayer you offered to me concerning Sennacherib, king of Assyria.
This is the word the Lord has spoken concerning him: The virgin daughter of Zion has despised you and scorned you; the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head at you.
Whom have you insulted and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice in insult and lifted your eyes on high? Against the Holy One of Israel!

Through your messengers you have insulted the Lord and said, ‘With my many chariots I climbed to the heights of the mountains, to the far reaches of Lebanon. I cut down its tall fir trees and its choicest cypresses, and I reached the farthest edge of the forest of Carmel.
I stored up and drank foreign waters, and with the soles of my feet I laid waste to all the mighty rivers.’
Have you not heard? Long ago I did this; in former days I fashioned it. I brought it to pass, and fortified cities became a boast for warriors who took captives.

Their inhabitants lost their strength, were terrified, and were put to shame. They became like the grass of the field, like green plants, like grass on rooftops, and like growth trampled down before it ripened.
Now I know your sitting down, your going out and your coming in, and your rage.
Because your anger against me and your exultation have reached my ears, I will put a hook in your nose and a bridle on your jaw, and I will turn you back by the road on which you came.

And this will be a sign for you: This year you will eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what grows of itself from that growth. In the third year, sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.
The surviving remnant of the house of Judah will again put down roots below and bear fruit above.
For a remnant will come out of Jerusalem, and survivors from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.
Therefore, thus says the Lord: The king of Assyria will not enter this city, shoot arrows into it, surround it with shields, or heap up earth against it.
He shall return by the same road by which he came, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord.
I will watch over this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.”
When night came, the angel of the Lord went out and struck down one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Assyrian camp. When they rose early in the morning, there were all the dead bodies.
Sennacherib king of Assyria departed, went away, and returned home, and he lived in Nineveh.

While he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword. They escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place.
In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “Thus says the Lord: Give instructions concerning your household, for you will die and will not live.”
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying,
“O Lord, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a wholehearted heart, and have done what is good in your sight.” And Hezekiah wept bitterly.
Isaiah was in the middle courtyard when the word of the Lord came to him, saying,

“Go back and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: Thus says the Lord, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayers and seen your tears. Look, I will heal you, and on the third day you will go up to the house of the Lord.
I will add fifteen years to your life, and I will rescue you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria. I will protect this city for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.”
Isaiah said, “Let them take cakes of figs.” And he took them. “Let them put them on your sore, and you will recover.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “What is the sign that the Lord will heal me and that I will go up to the house of the Lord on the third day?”
Isaiah said, “This is the sign from the Lord that the Lord will do what he has said: the shadow will move ten steps.”
Hezekiah said, “It is easy for the shadow to turn ten steps.” And he said, “Not that way! Rather, let the shadow turn backward ten steps.”
The prophet Isaiah cried out to the Lord, and the shadow turned backward ten steps, along the ten steps of Ahaz.
At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, because he had heard that Hezekiah had been ill.

Hezekiah was pleased with them and showed them all his treasure houses: the silver, the gold, the spices, the fragrant oils, the storehouses of equipment, and everything found in his treasuries. There was no place in his house or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them.
The prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and said to him, “What did those men say, and where did they come from to visit you?” Hezekiah said, “They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon.”
He said, “What did they see in your house?” Hezekiah said, “They saw everything that was in my house. There was nothing in my house that I did not show them, nor anything in my treasuries.”
Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the Lord:

Look, days are coming when everything in your house, and everything your ancestors have stored up to this day, will be taken away and carried to Babylon. Nothing will remain, for this is the word the Lord has spoken.
Some of your sons who will descend from you will be taken away, and they will become eunuchs in the house of the king of Babylon.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the Lord that he has spoken is good.” And he said, “Let there be peace and stability in my days.”

The rest of Hezekiah’s deeds, all his mighty acts, and how he made the water reservoirs and the water conduit and brought water into the city—are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
Hezekiah rested with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became king in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hephzibah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, following the abominations of the nations that the Lord had driven out before the Israelites.

He rebuilt the high places that his father Hezekiah had destroyed, erected an altar to Baal, and made a sacred grove, as Ahab king of Israel had done. He bowed down to all the host of heaven and served them.
He built an altar in the house of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had said, “In Jerusalem I will establish my throne.”
He built altars to all the host of heaven in all the courts of the house of the Lord.
He made his sons pass through fire, practiced divination, read omens from birds, and appointed mediums and diviners. He did much evil in the sight of the Lord, provoking him to anger.

He placed the carved images of the sacred groves in the house of the Lord, concerning which the Lord had said to David and his son Solomon, “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I will establish my name forever.

I will no longer make Israel's feet wander from the land that I gave their ancestors, provided they take care to do everything I commanded them, according to every command that my servant Moses gave them.”
But they did not listen, and Manasseh led them astray to do more evil in the sight of the Lord than the nations that the Lord had destroyed before the Israelites.
The Lord spoke through his servants the prophets, saying:
Because Manasseh, king of Judah, committed these evil abominations, worse than everything the Amorites did before me, and Judah sinned through their idols,
“Therefore, this is what the Lord, the God of Israel, says: Look, I am bringing disaster upon Jerusalem and Judah, so that both ears of everyone who hears of it will tingle.
I will stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line of Samaria and the plumb line of the house of Ahab. I will wipe Jerusalem clean like a bottle that is wiped clean and turned upside down.
I will reject the remnant of my inheritance and hand them over to their enemies. They shall become plunder and spoil for all their enemies.
This is because they have done evil in my sight and have provoked me to anger from the day I brought them out of Egypt until this day.”
Manasseh also shed a great deal of innocent blood, until he had filled Jerusalem from end to end, besides the sins by which he caused Judah to sin by doing evil in the sight of the Lord.
As for the rest of the acts of Manasseh, everything he did, and the sins he committed, are they not written in the book of the annals of the kings of Judah?
Manasseh rested with his ancestors and was buried in the garden of his house, in the garden of Uzziah. His son Amon became king in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for twelve years. His mother's name was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, as his father Manasseh had done.
He followed all the ways his father had followed, served the idols his father had served, and bowed down to them.
He abandoned the Lord, the God of his ancestors, and did not follow the ways of the Lord.
Amon's servants conspired against him and killed the king in his own house.
All the people struck down everyone who had conspired against King Amon, and the people of the land made his son Josiah king in his place.
As for the rest of the acts of Amon, what he did, are they not written in the book of the annals of the kings of Judah?
Amon rested with his ancestors, and they buried him in his tomb in the garden of Uzziah. His son Josiah became king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother's name was Jedidah, daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath.
He did what was right in the sight of the Lord and followed all the ways of his ancestor David, without turning aside to the right or to the left.
In the eighteenth year of Josiah, king of Judah, in the seventh month, the king sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, the chief scribe of the palace, saying,
Go to Hilkiah the high priest, so that they may melt down the silver brought into the house of the Lord, which the keepers collected by weight from the people.
Let them place it in the hands of the workers supervising the work on the house of the Lord. They gave it to the workers in the house of the Lord to repair the damage to the house of the Lord,
to the carpenters, builders, and craftsmen, to buy timber and dressed stones to repair the damage to the house of the Lord.
But they did not require an accounting of the silver given to them, because they worked faithfully.
Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the chief scribe, “I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord.” Hilkiah gave it to Shaphan, and he read it.

He brought the report to the king and said, “Your servants have melted down the silver found in the house of the Lord and placed it in the hands of the workers supervising the work in the house of the Lord.”
Shaphan the chief scribe spoke to the king and said, “Hilkiah the priest gave me a book.” Shaphan read it before the king.
When the king heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his clothes.
The king gave orders to Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the chief scribe, and Asaiah the king’s servant, saying,

“Go and inquire of the Lord for me, for all this people, and for all Judah concerning the words of this book that has been found. For the Lord’s great anger has been kindled against us because our fathers did not listen to the words of this book and do everything written in it concerning us.”

Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, [?] of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem, in Masena, and they spoke with her.
She said to them, “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Tell the man who sent you to me,
Thus says the Lord: Look, I am bringing disaster upon this place and its inhabitants, according to all the words of the book that the king of Judah read.
‘Because they abandoned me and burned incense to foreign gods, provoking me to anger with the works of their hands, my wrath will be kindled against this place and will not be extinguished.’
And to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, say this: ‘Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: These are the words you heard:

Because your heart softened and you humbled yourself before the Lord when you heard what he had spoken against this place and its inhabitants—that they would become a ruin and a curse—and because you tore your clothes and wept before me, I too have heard you, says the Lord.
Therefore I will gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your place in Jerusalem. Your eyes will not see all the disasters that I will bring upon this place.’”
They brought the report back to the king. The king sent and gathered to himself all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.

The king went up to the house of the Lord, and all the men of Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem were with him, along with the priests, the prophets, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. He read aloud to them all the words of the book of the covenant found in the house of the Lord.

The king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the Lord to follow the Lord and keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes with all his heart and all his soul, fulfilling the words of the covenant written in that book. All the people joined in the covenant.

The king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests of the second rank, and the keepers of the scales to bring out of the temple of the Lord all the vessels made for Baal, the sacred groves, and the host of heaven. He burned them outside Jerusalem, in Sademoth of Kidron, and carried their ashes to Bethel.

And he burned the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had appointed, who offered incense at the high places and in all the cities of Judah and around Jerusalem, and those who offered incense to the sun, the moon, the stars, and all the host of heaven.

And the sacred grove from the house of the Lord, outside Jerusalem, into the Kidron valley; and he burned it in the Kidron valley, ground it into dust, and scattered its ashes on the graves of the common people.
And he tore down the house of the sacred prostitutes that was in the house of the Lord, where the women wove robes for the sacred groves.

And he brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah and defiled the high places where the priests offered incense, from Geba to Beersheba. And he tore down the house of the gates beside the threshold of the gate of Joshua, the governor of the gate, on the left at the city gate.
But the priests of the high places did not go up to the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem; they only ate unleavened bread among their brothers.
And he defiled Topheth, which was in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, so that no one would make his son or daughter pass through the flame for Milcom.

And they burned the horses that the king of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance to the house of the Lord, by the treasury of Nathan, the king’s eunuch, which was in Parwarim. And he burned the chariots of the sun with fire.

The king tore down the altars on the roof of the upper room that the kings of Judah had made, and the altars that Manasseh had made in the two courts of the house of the Lord. He demolished them there and threw their dust into the Kidron ravine.

The king also defiled the house opposite Jerusalem, to the right of Mount Mosath, which Solomon king of Israel had built for Astarte, the abomination of the Sidonians, and for Chemosh, the detestable god of Moab, and for Milcom, the abomination of the Ammonites.
And he shattered the pillars, cut down the sacred groves, and filled their places with human bones.

And the altar at Bethel, the high place that Jeroboam son of Nebat, who caused Israel to sin, had made—he demolished that altar and high place as well, shattered its stones, ground them into dust, and burned the sacred grove.

And Josiah looked and saw the graves in the city. He sent men to take the bones from the graves, burned them on the altar, and defiled it, according to the word of the Lord that the man of God had spoken while Jeroboam stood at the altar during the festival. And he turned his eyes toward the grave of the man of God who had spoken these words.
And he said, “What is that monument I see?” The men of the city said to him, “It is the man of God who came from Judah and proclaimed these words against the altar of Bethel.”
He said, “Leave him alone; let no one disturb his bones.” His bones were found alongside the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria.

Josiah king of Israel also removed all the shrines of the high places in the cities of Samaria that the kings of Israel had made to provoke the Lord to anger. He did to them everything he had done at Bethel.
He burned all the priests of the high places who were there on the altars, and burned human bones on them. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
And the king commanded all the people, saying, “Celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God, as it is written in this book of the covenant.”
For no such Passover had been held since the days of the judges who judged Israel, or during the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.
But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah, this Passover was held to the Lord in Jerusalem.

And Josiah removed the mediums, the diviners, the household gods, the idols, and all the abominations that were in Judah and Jerusalem, to uphold the words of the law written in the book that Hilkiah the priest had found in the house of the Lord.

Before him there had been no king like him who turned to the Lord with all his heart, with all his soul, and with all his strength, according to all the law of Moses; nor did anyone like him arise after him.
Nevertheless, the Lord did not turn from his great and furious anger, with which he raged against Judah because of the provocations with which Manasseh had provoked him.
And the Lord said, “I will also cast Judah out of my presence, as I cast out Israel, and I will reject this city that I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name shall be there.’”
Now the rest of Josiah’s deeds and everything he did—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
In those days Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Assyria by the Euphrates River. King Josiah went out to meet him, and Pharaoh killed him at Megiddo when he saw him.

His servants carried him from Megiddo and brought him to Jerusalem, and they buried him in his own tomb. The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in place of his father.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done.
Pharaoh Neco removed him to Riblah in the land of Hamath so that he would not reign in Jerusalem, and imposed a tribute on the land of one hundred talents of silver and ten talents of gold.
Pharaoh Neco made Eliakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, king over them in place of his father Josiah, and changed his name to Jehoiakim. He took Jehoahaz and brought him to Egypt, where he died.

Jehoiakim gave the silver and gold to Pharaoh. But they carefully assessed the land to provide the silver at Pharaoh’s command. Each man, according to his assessment, together with the people of the land, gave silver and gold to be given to Pharaoh Neco.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Eldaph, daughter of Jeddel of Rumah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his ancestors had done.
In his days Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up, and Jehoiakim became his servant for three years. Then he turned and rebelled against him.

The Lord sent against him raiding bands of Chaldeans, raiding bands of Syrians, raiding bands of Moabites, and raiding bands of Ammonites. He sent them against the land of Judah to destroy it, according to the word of the Lord that he had spoken through his servants the prophets.
For the Lord’s anger was against Judah, to remove it from his presence because of the sins of Manasseh and everything he had done,
and because of the innocent blood he had shed. He had filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the Lord was unwilling to relent.
Now the rest of Jehoiakim’s deeds and everything he did—are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
Jehoiakim rested with his ancestors, and his son Jehoiachin reigned in his place.
The king of Egypt no longer came out of his land, because the king of Babylon had taken everything belonging to the king of Egypt, from the Wadi of Egypt to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem for three months. His mother’s name was Nehushta, daughter of Elamath of Jerusalem.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as his father had done.
At that time Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came up to Jerusalem, and the city came under siege.
The king of Babylon entered the city, while his servants kept it under siege.

Jehoiachin, king of Judah, went out to the king of Babylon, together with his servants, his mother, his officials, and his eunuchs. The king of Babylon took him captive in the eighth year of his reign.

He carried away all the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king’s house, and broke up all the gold vessels that Solomon, king of Israel, had made for the temple of the Lord, according to the word of the Lord.
He carried all Jerusalem into exile, along with all the officials and all the mighty warriors—ten thousand captives—and all the carpenters and smiths. No one remained except the poor of the land.
He carried Jehoiachin away to Babylon. He also led the king’s mother, his wives, his eunuchs, and the leading men of the land into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.
The king of Babylon led into exile in Babylon all the fighting men, seven thousand men, and the carpenters and smiths, one thousand men—all of them strong and fit for war.
The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, his son, king in his place and gave him the name Zedekiah.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did evil in the sight of the Lord, just as Jehoiakim had done.
For the Lord’s anger was against Jerusalem and Judah until he cast them out of his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

In the ninth year of his reign, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army. He encamped against it and built a siege wall all around it.
The city remained under siege until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah.
And until the ninth month, the famine grew severe in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land.

The city wall was breached, and all the fighting men went out by night along the road through the gate between the walls, beside the king’s garden. The Chaldeans were surrounding the city, and he went along the road to the Arabah.
The Chaldean army pursued the king closely and overtook him in the plains of Jericho. His whole army scattered away from him.
They captured the king and brought him to the king of Babylon at Riblah, and he passed judgment on him.
He killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes, blinded Zedekiah, bound him in chains, and took him to Babylon.

In the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, an attendant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He burned the house of the Lord, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem. He burned every house with fire.
The whole Chaldean army accompanying the captain of the guard tore down the walls around Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, deported the remaining people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the common people.
The captain of the guard left some of the poor of the land to work as vineyard keepers and farmers.
The Chaldeans broke up the two bronze pillars in the house of the Lord, the stands, and the bronze Sea in the house of the Lord, and carried their bronze to Babylon.
They took the pots, the cauldrons, the basins, the containers, and all the bronze utensils used in worship.
The captain of the guard took the censers and the dishes made of silver and gold.
And the two pillars, the one sea, and the stands that Solomon had made for the house of the Lord—the bronze of all these objects was beyond weighing.

One pillar was eighteen cubits high, with a bronze capital on top. The capital was three cubits high, and latticework and pomegranate-shaped ornaments surrounded the capital, all made of bronze. The second pillar was made in the same way, with latticework on it.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold.

From the city he took one eunuch who was in charge of the fighting men, five of the king’s attendants who were found in the city, the chief scribe and army officer who mustered the people of the land, and sixty other men from the people of the land who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
The king of Babylon struck them down and killed them at Riblah in the land of Hamath. And Judah was carried into exile from its land.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon left the people who remained in Judah and appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, over them.

All the commanders of his army and their men heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah over them. They came to Gedaliah at Mizpah: Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Sophathite, and Jaazaniah son of Maacah, together with their men.
They and their men swore an oath to Gedaliah, and he said to them, “Do not fear the raids of the Chaldeans. Stay in this land and serve the king of Babylon, and it will go well with you.”

In the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, of royal descent, came with ten men. They struck Gedaliah, and he died; they also struck the Jews and the Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.
All the people, from the least to the greatest, and the army commanders arose and went into Egypt, because they were afraid of the Chaldeans.

In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month, on the twenty-seventh day of the month, Evil-merodach king of Babylon, in the year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of his prison.
He spoke kindly to him and placed his throne above the thrones of the kings who were with him in Babylon.
He changed his prison clothes, and Jehoiachin ate continually in his presence all the days of his life.
His allowance was a regular allowance given to him from the king’s household, a daily portion, all the days of his life.
